html:
A painted limestone and plaster bust of Queen Nefertiti, made around 1345 BCE by the court sculptor Thutmose. It is one of the most copied works of ancient art and the best-known image of an Egyptian queen.

A German team led by Ludwig Borchardt found it in December 1912 in the ruins of Thutmose's workshop at Amarna, the capital built by her husband Akhenaten. The colours are almost intact; only the left eye has no inlay, perhaps because the bust was a model for other portraits. Its calm, balanced face shows the softer style of art under Atenism.

Under the rules then in force, finds were divided between Egypt and the diggers, and the bust went to Germany. It has been shown in Berlin since 1924 and now stands in the Neues Museum. Egypt has asked for it back many times, arguing that its value was hidden when the finds were shared out.
